newsitem.title: FRANCE: French insurance merger revives financial sector.
newsitem.headline: French insurance merger revives financial sector.

text.p: France on Wednesday declared itself proud possessor of a future heavyweight in world finance as news of the multi-billion dollar merger between insurers Axa and UAP revived interest in French banks and the banking sector.
How long the euphoria lasts from creating the world's second biggest insurer is a different question, but the revival factor is genuine.
"This proves the ability and willingness of French companies to compete on a worldwide scale," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told the National Assembly on Wednesday.

When Axa and Union des Assurances de Paris (UAP) merge next year, they will create the second largest insurer in the world after Nippon Life Insurance Co of Japan and the world's largest asset management group.

Investment analysts and share traders, impressed with the prospects of the new group, began a hard look at other financial sector players on Wednesday, with eyes turning to the recently privatised insurer AGFand CCFbank in particular.
"People are looking at the financial sector. There's been quite a few things happening. CCF has been mentioned as a target many times," one banking analyst said.
"It's a good bank but probably not quite big enough," one trader suggested.
Shares in Credit Commercial de France (CCF) surged more than three percent in value during the day before settling 2.09 percent higher at 248.8 francs each.

The new-found optimism spilled over to other banks as well with shares in Societe Generale and Paribas gaining 2.29 percent and 1.17 percent respectively on a turn in sentiment, bucking a generally downward trend on the Paris bourse.
"Societe Generale has been a big underperformer, there seems to be a big push to financials," one analyst said.
While BNP, another major French bank, lost ground, this was put down to profit-taking after a surge or more than eight percent on Tuesday.
On the insurance front, analysts turned their attention to AGF, which was privatised by the government in July.
"Some observers believe AGF could be a target. The question is whose target," another Paris financial analyst said.
Names thrown up include Italy's Generaliand Allianz, the German company which will be pushed out of the top place in European insurance by the Axa/UAP duo.
Others suggest AGF could possibly seek an alliance with a medium-sized French insurer such as Athena.
However, those hoping for a spate of merger and acquisition activity that would totally transform the face of the French financial sector may be disappointed.

At least up until Tuesday when the Axa/UAP deal surfaced, the more widespread belief among analysts is that restructuring will be a protracted process of gradual regulatory reform and state withdrawal from the banking and insurance sector.
The government, under mounting pressure from the big private banks, is studying ways of ending regulatory distortions to "level the playing field" and is also planning a string of privatisations.

First in the sell-off line is CIC, a regional banking group owned by state-controlled insurer Groupe des Assurances Nationales (GAN). That sale is supposed to generate enough money for GAN to be privatised itself.
Then, the mammoth task facing the government is the sell-off of Credit Lyonnais, which mounted a catastrophic expansion spree in the 1980s that nearly drove it into bankruptcy.
